column2: The fruit declared for month-long fasts duly observed, a man obtains by seeing Krishna on the platform.
What need to say more, repeating it again and again, about the greatness of that god on the platform, O best of brahmins?
The fruit declared for vows and gifts at all holy places, the doer of good obtains by seeing Krishna on the platform with the plough-armed one
and Subhadra, O best of sages. Therefore man or woman should see that Purushottama;
then one obtains the fruit of bathing and the rest at all holy places. With the water remaining from Krishna's bath one anoints oneself.
A barren woman, one whose children have died, the unfortunate, one afflicted by planets, one seized by Rakshasas and the like, or those beset by diseases —
anointed at once with the water remaining from the bath, they obtain whatever desires they wish.
One seeking a son obtains sons, one seeking happiness obtains good fortune, the sick is freed from disease, and one wanting wealth obtains wealth.
All the holy waters that exist on the earth are not worth a sixteenth part of the water remaining from the bath.
Therefore, O brahmins, one should anoint one's limbs with the water remaining from Krishna's bath, for it grants every desire.
Those who see Krishna, after his bath, going toward the south are freed from sins such as brahmin-slaying; there is no doubt.
The fruit declared in the scriptures for circumambulating the earth three times, a man obtains by seeing Krishna going toward the south.
The fruit declared for pilgrimage to holy places on earth, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit declared at Badari for seeing Nara and Narayana, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit of bathing and giving at Gangadvara and Kurukshetra, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit declared at Prayaga on the great Magha full moon, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit of bathing and giving at Shalagrama on the great Chaitra full moon, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit remembered at Pushkara on the great Karttika full moon, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit of bathing and giving at the confluence of the Ganga and the sea, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
The fruit of bathing and giving at Kurukshetra during a solar eclipse, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
In the Ganga, at all holy places, at the holy places of the Yamuna, O brahmins, at the holy places of the Sarasvati and in other lakes,
the fruit declared for bathing and giving duly, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
At Pushkara and other holy places, at Gaya and Amarakantaka, at Naimisha and other holy places, regions and shrines,
the fruit of bathing and giving when the sun is seized by Rahu, a man obtains by seeing Krishna facing south.
What need to say it again and again? Whatever fruit of meritorious action has been told here,
in the Vedas and scriptures, in the Puranas and the Bharata, O best of brahmins, in all the law books and elsewhere by the wise,
a man obtains all that fruit by seeing Krishna with the plough-armed one and Bhadra, going toward the south.
One should mentally recite a hundred and eight times the purifying goddess Gayatri, mother of the Vedas, holy and removing all sins,
and the holy solar mantras, with faith and composure; then, having circumambulated three times, one should bow to the sun.
Bathing and recitation according to the Veda are prescribed for the three classes; for women and shudras, bathing and recitation without the Vedic procedure.
Then, silent, one should go home and worship Purushottama, having washed hands and feet and sipped water according to rule.
One should bathe the god with ghee, then with milk, with honey and fragrant water, and with sacred water and sandal-water.
Then one should devotedly clothe him in an excellent pair of garments and anoint him with sandal, aloe, camphor and saffron.
One should worship Purushottama with supreme devotion with lotuses, and with other Vaishnava flowers such as mallika.
Having thus worshipped Hari, lord of the world, giver of enjoyment and liberation, one should burn incense with aloe before the god,
and fragrant guggulu, O best of sages; one should light a lamp with ghee devotedly according to one's ability,
and with composure give twelve other lamps, with ghee, O best of sages, or with sesame oil.
As food offering one should offer milk-rice, cakes, fried cakes, vatakas, sweet balls, a little molasses and fruits.
Having thus worshipped Purushottama with the fivefold service, one should recite "Salutation to Purushottama" a hundred and eight times.
Then one should devotedly propitiate the god Purushottama: "Salutation to you, lord of all worlds, giver of fearlessness to devotees;
save me, sunk in the ocean of worldly existence, O Purushottama. The twelve pilgrimages I have made to you, O lord of the world,
by your grace, O Govinda, may they be complete for me." Having thus propitiated the god and prostrated like a staff,
one should then worship the teacher devotedly with flowers, garments and unguents, since there is no difference between the two, O best of sages.
With faith and composure one should make above the god a variegated pavilion of various flowers, O best of sages.
Having made the dedication, one should then hold a vigil at night and have the story of Vasudeva and songs performed.
The wise one should pass the night meditating, reading and praising the god. Then at clear dawn on the twelfth day, twelve
brahmins who have completed their vows, masters of the Veda, knowers of the Itihasas and Puranas, learned and self-controlled, should be invited.
Having bathed properly by rule, in washed garments and with senses controlled, one should bathe the god as before and worship Purushottama there,
with perfumes, flowers, presents, food offerings and lamps, with services of many kinds, prostrations and circumambulations,
with recitations, hymns, salutations and charming songs and music; having thus worshipped the lord of the world, one should then honour the brahmins.
Having given them twelve cows and gold, an umbrella and a pair of sandals, with faith and devotion,
one should devotedly give them garments and the like along with wealth, O brahmins, for Govinda is pleased when worshipped with sincerity.
Then one should devotedly give the teacher a cow, garments and gold, an umbrella, a pair of sandals and a bronze vessel.
Then one should feed those brahmins with food beginning with milk-rice, cooked food, foods to chew and eat, with molasses and ghee.
Then, when the brahmins are satisfied with food and content in mind, one should give them twelve water-jars with sweets,
and without envy give them a fee according to one's ability; one should present a jar and a fee to the teacher.
Having thus honoured those brahmins, one should worship with supreme devotion the teacher who imparts knowledge, as equal to Vishnu, O best of brahmins.
The wise one, having worshipped him with gold, garments, cows, grain and other excellent things and bowed to him, should utter this mantra:
May the all-pervading lord of the world, bearer of conch, discus and mace, the god without beginning or end, Purushottama, be pleased.
Having uttered this and circumambulated the brahmins three times, bowing the head with devotion, one should dismiss the teacher.
Then one should devotedly follow those brahmins up to the boundary; having followed them all, one should bow and return.
Then, with kinsmen and one's own people, one should eat in silence, along with other worshippers, the poor, mendicants and those seeking food.
Having done this properly, a man or woman obtains the fruit of a thousand horse sacrifices and a hundred Rajasuya sacrifices.
Taking with him a hundred past generations and a hundred future ones, O best of men, O brahmins, by going to heaven he bears a divine form,
endowed with every good mark, adorned with every ornament, rich in every desire, free of fever like a god,
endowed with beauty and youth, adorned with all virtues, praised by Apsarases and adorned by Gandharvas,
in a celestial car coloured like the sun, moving at will and steady, with flags and banners, adorned with all jewels,
illuminating all directions in the sky, free from weariness, young, mighty and wise, he goes to Vishnu's world.
There for a hundred kalpas he enjoys pleasures as he wishes, praised by Siddhas, Apsarases, Gandharvas, gods, Vidyadharas and serpents,
and by the best of sages he remains free of fever. As the god, lord of the world, bearing conch, discus and mace,
so he, joyful, O brahmins, takes a four-armed form; having enjoyed excellent pleasures there and sported with the gods,
at its end he comes to the abode of Brahma, which grants every desire, beautiful with Siddhas, Vidyadharas, gods and Kinnaras.
Having enjoyed happiness there for ninety kalpas, from there, O best of brahmins, he comes to the world that grants the fruit of every desire,
the world of Rudra, frequented by hosts of gods, giving happiness and liberation, adorned with many hundreds of thousands of celestial cars,
adorned with Siddhas, Vidyadharas, Yakshas, Daityas and Danavas; having enjoyed happiness there for eighty kalpas,
at its end he goes to Goloka, endowed with every enjoyment, beautiful and charming with gods, Siddhas and Apsarases.
Having enjoyed there for seventy kalpas unsurpassed enjoyment, rare in the three worlds, content in mind like an immortal,
from there he comes to the unsurpassed world of Prajapati, surrounded by Gandharvas, Apsarases, Siddhas, sages and Vidyadharas.
Having joyfully enjoyed various happiness there for sixty kalpas, at its end he comes to the abode of Shakra, full of various wonders,
with Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, gods, Vidyadharas and serpents, Guhyakas, Apsarases, Sadhyas and other excellent gods.
Coming there, the man enjoys happiness for fifty kalpas; then going to the world of the gods, adorned with celestial cars,
having enjoyed very rare pleasures for forty kalpas, he then comes to the very rare world called that of the stars.
There he enjoys excellent pleasures for thirty kalpas as he wishes; from there he comes to the world of the moon, O best of brahmins,
where Soma dwells, adorned by all the gods; having enjoyed very rare pleasure there for twenty kalpas,
he then comes to the world of the sun, worshipped by the gods, full of various wonders, holy, frequented by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having enjoyed auspicious pleasures there for ten kalpas, O best of brahmins, from there he comes to the very rare world of the Gandharvas.
Having enjoyed all pleasures there as he likes for one kalpa, he comes to the earth and becomes a righteous king,
a universal emperor of great valour, adorned with all virtues; having ruled according to his dharma and performed sacrifices with good fees,
at its end he goes to the auspicious world of yogins that grants liberation; having enjoyed excellent pleasures there until the dissolution of beings,
he comes from there and is born here in a family of yogins, an excellent Vaishnava family, O brahmins, rare and esteemed by the good,
a foremost brahmin learned in the four Vedas; having performed sacrifices with proper fees and taking up the yoga of Vishnu, he then attains liberation.
Thus, O brahmins, I have properly described the fruit of pilgrimage, which grants enjoyment and liberation to men. What else do you wish to hear?
With cars swift as mind and wind, crowded with clusters of bells, they roam in that city of Vishnu worshipped by the world,
constantly with various women, Gandharvas, Apsarases and others, with lovely moon-faced women, very charming,
with full, raised breasts and fine waists all around, youthful and fair, walking like intoxicated elephants;
surrounding the best of men, those women fanned him with chowries with golden handles adorned with various jewels,
with songs, dances and music, joyful and languid with intoxication; with Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Siddhas, Gandharvas, hosts of Apsarases,
hosts of gods and sages, the best of worlds shone. Reaching there, the wise obtain great enjoyments —
those by whom the Lord Krishna, lotus-eyed lord of the world, was seen near the king of banyans on the shore of the southern ocean.
They sport with Apsarases as long as heaven, moon and stars endure, like molten gold, free from old age and death,
free from all sorrow, free from craving and weariness, four-armed, very mighty, adorned with forest garlands,
marked with the Shrivatsa, bearing conch, discus and mace; some dark as blue lotuses, some like gold,
some like emerald, some like beryl, some dark and wearing earrings, and others like diamond.
The worlds of all the gods do not shine as the world of Hari shines, full of all wonders, O best of brahmins.
There is no return from going there, O brahmins; by the power of that god, until the dissolution of beings,
they roam in the divine city, proud of beauty and youth, and see Krishna, Rama and Subhadra at Purushottama.
In the middle of the city shines Hari's temple, like molten gold, like the young sun, adorned with jewels,
adorned with many hundreds of thousands of banners, ten thousand yojanas wide and surrounded by a golden rampart,
with variegated flags of various colours, very charming, it shines like the autumn moon with the stars.
With four gates, very broad, well guarded by chamberlains, joined with seven enclosures, very lofty and charming —
the first of gold, the second set with emeralds, the third of sapphire, and after that of great sapphire,
the fifth enclosure blazing and made of rubies, the sixth of diamond, O brahmins, and the seventh of beryl.
That great mansion shines with wondrous pillars made of various gems and adorned with gold and coral shoots.
Siddhas are seen there illuminating the ten directions, as the moon shines with the stars on the full-moon night.
Seated there is the Lord Janardana with Lakshmi, clad in yellow, dark, marked with the Shrivatsa.
Hari held in his right hand the blazing, terrible Sudarshana discus, chief of all weapons, made of all splendour.
Taking in his left hand, O best of sages, the conch like jasmine, the moon and silver, like a necklace and cow's milk,
at whose sound the whole world is shaken, famed as Panchajanya, adorned with a thousand spirals,
and the fierce mace Kaumodaki, ender of evil-doers, destroyer of Daityas and Danavas, like a blazing flame of fire, unbearable even to the gods,
he held in his right hand; in his left flashes his Sharnga bow, radiant as the sun,
with which, with excellent arrows like the sun wreathed in flames, that god destroys the three worlds with all that moves and does not move.
The glorious one who gives all bliss, skilled in all scriptures, the god who is teacher of all worlds, saluted by all the gods,
the thousand-headed lord of the gods, with a thousand feet and eyes, a thousand names, a thousand limbs, the Lord with a thousand arms,
the god seated on the throne, with eyes long as lotus petals, clear as lightning, lord of the world, teacher of the world,
surrounded by gods and Siddhas, hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases, Yakshas, Vidyadharas, Nagas, sages, Siddhas and Charanas,
Suparnas, Danavas, Daityas, Rakshasas, Guhyakas, Kinnaras and other divine hosts of gods — praised by them, he shines.
There always dwell Kirti, Prajna, Medha, Sarasvati, Buddhi, Mati, Kshanti, Siddhimurti and Dyuti,
Gayatri, Savitri, Mangala, Sarvamangala, Prabha, Mati and Kanti; Narayani dwells there,
and Shraddha, the goddess Kaushiki, Vidyut, Saudamini, Nidra, Ratri, Maya and other immortal women —
all of them are established in Vasudeva's abode. What need to say more? Everything is established there.
Ghritachi, Menaka, Rambha, Sahajanya, Tilottama, Urvashi, Nimlocha, another, and Vamana,
Mandodari, Subhaga, Vishvachi, Vipulanana, Bhadrangi, Chitrasena and the very charming Pramlocha,
Munisammohini, Rama, Chandramadhya, Shubhanana, Sukeshi, Nilakesha and Manmathadipini,
Alambusha, Mishrakeshi, another Munjikasthala, Kratusthala, Varangi and Purvachitti,
Paravati, Maharupa, Shashilekha, Shubhanana, following the gait of swans and walking like intoxicated elephants,
Bimbaushthi and Navagarbha — famed women of the gods; these and other Apsarases, proud of beauty and youth,
slender-waisted, lovely-faced, adorned with every ornament, with sweet song, endowed with every good mark,
skilled in song and music, women of gods and Gandharvas, dance daily there where Purushottama is.
There is no disease there, no weariness, no death, no cold or heat, no hunger or thirst, no old age, no ugliness and no unhappiness.
I see no world here higher than the world of Vishnu, which produces supreme bliss and grants the fruit of every desire, O brahmins.
The worlds of those of meritorious deeds heard of in heaven are not worth a sixteenth part of the world of Vishnu, O brahmins.
Thus is Hari's city, endowed with all enjoyments and virtues, bringing all happiness, holy, full of every wonder, O brahmins.
Atheists do not go there, nor men absorbed in sense-objects, nor the ungrateful, the slanderous, thieves or those with senses uncontrolled.
Those Vaishnavas who always worship Vasudeva, teacher of the world, with devotion, go there to Vishnu's world; there is no doubt.
Having seen Krishna, Rama and Subhadra in the most rare region on the shore of the southern ocean, O best of brahmins,
those men who give up their bodies near the wish-fulfilling tree, who die at Purushottama, go there.
Those who remember Purushottama between the banyan and the ocean, those men who die at Purushottama, also go there.
They too go to that supreme abode; there is no doubt. Thus, O best of sages, I have told you of the eternal world of Vishnu, which gives all bliss and grants the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
True, true, O best of sages, is what you have declared: there is no region on the earth equal to the one called Purusha.
The holy places and sacred shrines that exist are not worth a sixteenth part of the one called Shri Purusha.
As Vishnu, lord of all, is the highest of all worlds, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Vishnu is declared the best among the Adityas, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the moon among the stars and the ocean among lakes, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As fire among the Vasus and Shankara among the Rudras, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the brahmin among the classes and Vainateya among birds, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Meru among peaks and the Himalaya among mountains, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Lakshmi among women and the Jahnavi among rivers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Airavata among lordly elephants and Bhrigu among great sages, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Skanda among generals and Kapila among the perfected, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Uchchaihshravas among horses and the seer Ushanas among seers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Vyasa among sages and Kubera among Yakshas and Rakshasas, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the mind among the senses and the earth among the elements, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the ashvattha among all trees and the wind among moving things, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the crest-jewel among all ornaments, O brahmins, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Chitraratha among Gandharvas and the thunderbolt among weapons, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the letter A among all letters and the Gayatri among metres, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the head is the best of all limbs, O best of brahmins, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Arundhati has attained pre-eminence among chaste women, so is that Purushottama the best of all holy places.
As the knowledge of liberation is remembered as supreme among all knowledge, so is that Purushottama the best of all holy places.
As the king among men and the wish-granting cow among cows, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As gold among all precious things and Vasuki among serpents, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Prahlada among all Daityas and Rama among wielders of weapons, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the makara among fishes and the lion among beasts, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the milk ocean is the best of oceans, lord of rivers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Varuna among aquatic creatures and Yama among restrainers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Narada is the best of divine sages, O best of sages, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As gold among metals and the sacrificial fee among purifiers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As Daksha among lords of creatures and Kashyapa among seers, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the sun among the planets and the pranava among mantras, so Purushottama is the best of all holy places.
As the horse sacrifice is declared the best of sacrifices, so is that region among all holy places, O best of brahmins.
As grain among plants and the king of grasses among grasses, so Purushottama is the highest of all holy places.
As dharma, which carries one across worldly existence, is best among all holy things, so is that Purushottama the best of all holy places.
There are the holy places I have told you of: between the Himalaya and the Vindhya there are six rivers of divine origin,
and likewise, O Brahman, divine ones between the southern ocean and the Vindhya; these twelve rivers are declared as the principal ones.
Because Bharata, bestowing much merit, is worshipped by the gods as the land of action, it is therefore declared a varsha.
The holy places of the sages and those of the gods were in places covered by Asuras; hence those are called Asuric.
In the divine regions the great sages practised austerity; by the power of the gods and of austerity, those too became holy places of the sages.
For their own good, for liberation, for worship or prosperity, for the fruit and prosperity of themselves, or again to obtain fame,
those made by men are called human, O Narada. Thus there are four kinds of holy places, O best of sages.
No one knows the distinction; you are fit to hear it, O Narada. Many who think themselves learned hear and speak, but only some rare virtuous person knows how to tell and hear it by his own merits.

I wish to hear truly their nature and distinctions, hearing which one is freed from all sins; there is no doubt.
brahmapuran:70:31	O Brahman, from the beginning of the Krita age there is no other means, apart from resorting to holy places, that grants one's desire with little effort.
brahmapuran:70:32	O Creator, there is no speaker or knower anywhere like you; you were born in the navel-lotus of Vishnu, the forefather of all.
The Godavari, Bhimarathi, Tungabhadra, Venika, Tapi and Payoshni are declared to the south of the Vindhya;
the Bhagirathi, Narmada, Yamuna, Sarasvati, Vishoka and Vitasta rest on the Himalaya mountains.
These most holy rivers are declared divine holy places. Gaya, Kollasura, Vritra, Tripura and Andhaka,
Hayamurdha, Lavana, Namuchi, Shringaka, Yama, Patalaketu, Maya and Pushkara —
holy places covered by these are Asuric, yet auspicious. Prabhasa, Bhargava, Agasti, Nara and Narayana,
Vasishtha, Bharadvaja, Gotama, Kashyapa, Manu — those frequented by such sages are the holy places of the sages, O Narada.
Ambarisha, Harishchandra, Mandhata, Manu, Kuru, Kanakhala, Bhadrashva and Sagara,
Ashvayupa, Nachiketas, Vrishakapi and Arindama — by such men, O brahmin, auspicious ones were made,

made here for the sake of fame, fruit and prosperity, O Narada. The divine ones arose of themselves anywhere in the three worlds; they are called holy places of merit. Thus I have told the distinction of holy places.
Worshipped by the lord of the world, the mighty Vishnu, Mainaka, the best of mountains, shone exceedingly golden.
The sages, the guardians of the worlds, the Adityas and the hosts of Maruts made the altar for the wedding of the trident-bearing god of gods.
Vishvakarman, Tvashtri himself, made the altar with archways. Surabhi, Nandini, Nanda, Sunanda and Kamadohini —
adorned by these, the wedding of Ishani took place. The oceans, rivers, Nagas, plants and mothers of the world,
with trees and seeds, all came there. Ila did the work of the earth, the plants the work of food,
Varuna the work of drinks, and the lord of wealth the work of gifts; Agni prepared there the food that the lords of the world liked.
The eternal Vishnu performed separate worship here and there; and the Vedas with their secrets sang and laughed.
All the Apsarases danced, the Gandharvas and Kinnaras sang, and Mainaka held the parched grain, O best of sages.
The recitation of auspicious-day blessings took place in the inner apartment, O Narada; the divine couple, best of gods, sat on the altar.
Having duly established the fire and the stone, my son, and offered parched grain duly, he then performed the circumambulation.
For the touching of the stone, prompted by Vishnu, Shambhu took in his hand the big toe of the Goddess's right foot.
I saw it there while performing the fire offering near Hara; seeing the toe with a wicked mind, my seed then flowed.
Stained with shame, I crushed the fallen seed; from my fine crushed seed the Valakhilyas were born.
Then a great cry of dismay arose there from the gods; overcome with shame, I left my seat.
As the hosts of gods looked on in silence, O Narada, Mahadeva, seeing me going, said to Nandin:
Call Brahma here; I will free him from sin. The good are compassionate even to one who has offended; such is the nature of sense-objects that they bewilder even the learned.
Having said this, that Lord Shiva with Uma, out of compassion for me and wishing the good of the worlds,
the lord of the world did this — hear it carefully, O Narada: "Earth and water will be for the release of sinners from sin.
I will take the purifying essence of both." Having resolved thus, the Lord gathered their essence.
Making the earth into a water-pot and placing the waters in it, consecrating it carefully with the Pavamani and other hymns,
the destroyer of sin remembered there the power that purifies the three worlds. The lord of the world said to me, "Take this water-pot.
The waters are divine mothers, and the earth is another mother; the causes of sustenance, origin and destruction rest in both.
Here dharma is established, here the eternal sacrifice, here enjoyment and liberation, the unmoving and the moving.
By remembrance mental sin is destroyed, by speech verbal sin, and by bathing, drinking and sprinkling even bodily sin.
This alone is nectar in the world; there is nothing more purifying than it. Consecrated by me, O Brahman, take this water-pot.
Whoever even remembers or recites the water in it obtains all desires; take this water-pot.
Of the five elements, water is declared the great element; this is the most excellent of waters; take this water-pot.
By touching, remembering and seeing the most beautiful, holy and purifying water in it, O Brahman, you will be freed from sin."
Having said this, Mahadeva gave me the water-pot. Then all the hosts of gods praised the lord of gods with devotion; great joy arose there and the cry of victory went forth.

At the festival of the gods the unborn one, having looked at the tip of the mother's foot, fell into sin; the compassionate father gave him the Ganga, purifying by mere remembrance, held in the holy water-pot.
Saying "So be it," the hosts of gods went to heaven, and the Lord, the lord of gods, entered Aditi's womb.
When he was being born, festivals took place; that Vamana was born, O Brahman, lord of sacrifice, the Person of sacrifice.
Meanwhile, O Brahman, Bali, best of the mighty, was consecrated for a horse sacrifice, attended by the chief sages,
with Shukra as priest, knower of the Vedas and their limbs. As that sacrifice proceeded, with Bali as sacrificer,
with the chief sages as officiants and Shukra as priest, and gods, Gandharvas and serpents present for their share of oblations,
while the words "Let it be given, let it be eaten, let worship be done separately; it is complete, again complete" went on,
slowly Vamana came to that place, singing the Saman; Vamana with bright earrings reached the sacrificial enclosure,
praising that sacrifice. Seeing Vamana, the Bhargava — the god in the form of a brahmin, Vamana, slayer of Daityas,
giver of the fruit of sacrifices and austerities, slayer of Rakshasas — recognising him, hastily spoke to the king of great splendour,
conqueror by the kshatriya dharma, giver of wealth with devotion, Bali, best of the mighty, consecrated for the sacrifice with his wife,
meditating on the Person of sacrifice and offering oblations separately; to him spoke Shukra, tiger of the Bhrigus, of supreme intelligence:

The brahmin in the form of a dwarf who has come to your sacrifice is truly not a brahmin, O Bali; he is the lord of sacrifice, the bearer of sacrifice.
brahmapuran:73:33	This child has surely come to beg from you for the good of the gods. Only after consulting with me should you give, O lord.
But Bali, subduer of foes, said to the Bhargava, his priest:
I am blessed that the lord of sacrifice comes in embodied form to my house. Having come, he asks for something — what remains to consult about?
Having said this, with his wife and the priest Shukra, he went where the best of brahmins, Vamana, son of Aditi, was.
With joined palms he said, "Tell me what you seek." Then Vamana said, "Land measured by three steps —
give me that, O king of kings; I have no need of any other wealth." Saying "So be it," from pitchers adorned with various gems,
pouring a stream of water, he gave the land to Vamana, while the chief sages and the priest Shukra looked on;
while the lords of the worlds looked on, he gave the land to Vamana; while the hosts of Daityas looked on, the cry of victory arose.
Slowly Vamana said, "Hail, O king, be happy; give me the measured land of three steps; it is to be traversed at once."
So be it, said the lord of the Daityas; as he looked at Vamana, the lord of sacrifice, the Person of sacrifice, so that the moon and sun were at his breast
and the gods at his head, grew into the striding form; the endless, imperishable god, the strider of the striding form. Seeing him, the king of Daityas with his wife said humbly:
Stride, O Vishnu, lord of the world, as far as your power goes, O you who are the universe; I have been conquered wholly, O lord of the gods, maker of the universe.
At the very moment of his words, Vishnu, the great sacrifice, said:
O mighty-armed lord of the Daityas, I will stride; watch, O king of the Daityas.
As he spoke thus, the other said, "Stride, Vishnu," again and again.
Placing his foot on the tortoise's back, he placed a step at Bali's sacrifice; the second step reached the eternal world of Brahma.
There is no place here for the third step, O lord of the Asuras; where shall I stride? Give me land, said Hari to Bali. Bali, with his wife, joined his palms and, smiling, said:

The whole world was created by you; I am not its creator, O lord of the gods. By your fault it has become small; what can I do, O you who are the universe?
brahmapuran:73:51	Yet I have never before spoken falsely, O Keshava; making my word true, place your step on my back.
Then the Lord, whose form is the three Vedas, worshipped by the gods, was pleased:
Choose a boon, blessings on you; I am pleased with your devotion, O king of the Daityas.
He said to the lord of the world, "I ask nothing of you, O Trivikrama." But Vishnu himself, pleased, gave him what his heart desired:
lordship of Rasatala and the future position of Indra again, mastery of himself and imperishable fame, the all-pervading Hari gave.
Having thus given everything to Bali and established Bali, enemy of the immortals, with his sons and wife in Rasatala,
Hari gave the kingship of the gods to Shatakratu as it had been. Meanwhile the step, worshipped by the gods, came there —
that second step of Vishnu, my father, O wise one; seeing the step reach my house, I reflected:

What should be done that would be auspicious for me, now that Vishnu's foot has come? Surveying all my possessions, the best for me is my water-pot,
brahmapuran:73:60	the water which is most holy, given by the enemy of Tripura — excellent, most adorable, boon-giving, supreme, bringing peace,
brahmapuran:73:61	auspicious and ever bestowing auspiciousness, granting enjoyment and liberation, the mother of the worlds in form, nectar, medicine, pure,
brahmapuran:73:62	holy, purifying, worshipful, eldest, best and full of virtues — purifying people merely by remembrance, how much more by sight?
brahmapuran:73:63	Being pure, I will prepare such water as an offering to my father. Having reflected thus, he took that water and prepared it as an offering.
The offering-water, well consecrated, fell on Vishnu's foot; that water fell on Meru and went to the earth in four directions,
east, south, west and north. What fell in the south, O sage, Shankara received in his matted locks;
what fell in the west went back into the water-pot; the water that fell in the north Vishnu received;
in the east the sages, gods, ancestors and guardians of the worlds received the auspicious water; therefore it is called the best.
The waters, mothers of the world, that reached the southern direction, born from Vishnu's foot, friendly to brahmins, mothers of the world,
resting in Maheshvara's matted locks, arising auspiciously at festivals — by remembering their power one attains all desires.
Only when the brahmin Gautama gives and offers oblations is there sustenance in heaven, even for the gods, and not otherwise.
In the world of the gods and among mortals the sage Gautama is spoken of; people know that he alone is the offerer, the giver and the enjoyer.
Hearing that, all the sages dwelling in various hermitages, ascetics, came asking for Gautama's hermitage.
To all those sages who came, that Gautama became a nourisher with devotion, like a disciple, like a son, like a father.
The sage served all of them according to each one's desire, as fitting, in due order and as suitable.
At Gautama's command the plants, mothers of the world, were there, and Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara were worshipped by him again.
The plants were born then and reaped then; they were sown then and ripened, by the power of Gautama's austerity.
All prosperities that he wished for in his mind were accomplished. Every day Gautama humbly said to the sages who had come:
Like a son, like a disciple, like a servant — what shall I do? He nourished them like a father for many years.
While the sages dwelt there thus, the hermitage gained fame in the three worlds. Then Vinayaka spoke to his mother, his brother and Jaya:

Mother, in the abode of the gods the brahmin Gautama is sung of: 'Gautama has done what the hosts of gods could not accomplish.'
brahmapuran:74:40	Thus I have heard, O Goddess, of that brahmin's power of austerity. That brahmin could bring down this Ganga who dwells in the matted locks, Mother.
brahmapuran:74:41	By austerity or otherwise, having worshipped the three-eyed god, he alone could bring down this one in the locks, dear to my father.
brahmapuran:74:42	A strategy must be devised so that the brahmin asks for her; by his power the best of rivers would descend from the head.
Having said this to his mother, the lord of obstacles, with his brother and Jaya, went to where Gautama, lean and wearing the sacred thread, was.
Staying some days in the region of Gautama's hermitage, the lord of obstacles said to all the brahmins here and there:
Let us go to our own dwellings and pure hermitages; we have been nourished by Gautama's food; let us ask leave of the sage Gautama.
Having agreed on this, the excellent sages asked him; he restrained those sages one by one out of affection,
with joined palms and humility: "Stay here indeed; I will serve your feet, O bulls among sages."
